title: Why normalize?
text: Divide an embedding by its L2 norm to make its length one. The dot product of two unit vectors equals their cosine similarity.
credit: Passage written for this course

title: The CLIP training loss
text: CLIP compares each image with every caption in a batch. Row and column softmaxes form two distributions. The loss averages the negative log probabilities of the observed image-caption partners.
credit: Passage written for this course

title: Retrieval and generation
text: An embedding model finds relevant source passages. A separate generative model can use those passages to write an answer. A high retrieval score is not a guarantee that the passage answers the question.
credit: Passage written for this course

title: The text readout in original CLIP
text: Original CLIP uses causal self-attention in its text Transformer. The end-of-text token can attend to the whole preceding description. Its final state provides the text representation.
credit: Passage written for this course

title: Shorter vectors
text: With Matryoshka embeddings, keep the first 512, 256, or 128 coordinates, then normalize again. Shorter vectors save index memory. Multimodal retrieval at 128 dimensions can lose quality.
credit: Passage written for this course

title: Solar power
text: Photovoltaic panels convert sunlight into electrical energy. Solar farms arrange many panels in rows. Power production varies with sunlight and cloud cover.
credit: Passage written for this course

title: Elephant Island by Landsat 8
credit: NASA Earth Observatory image by Joshua Stevens, using Landsat data from the U.S. Geological Survey. Story by Kasha Patel. · Public domain · Commons thumbnail, resized.
description:
When explorer Ernest Shackleton and the crew of Endurance lost their ship to crushing pack ice in the Weddell Sea in 1915, their chances of survival seemed dim. The 28 men spent months drifting on ice floes and traversing the Southern Ocean in small lifeboats until they finally spotted land. The hunk of rock and ice was not the welcoming refuge they hoped for, but it was enough.
Shackleton and the crew of the Imperial Trans-Antarctic expedition landed on the mountainous, ice-covered island today

title: 2016-11-13 01 Kjeungskjær Lighthouse, Sør-Trøndelag, Norway
credit: Gordon Leggett · CC BY-SA 4.0 · Commons thumbnail, resized.
description:
Kjeungskjær Lighthouse (sometimes called The Red Sailor), at Sør-Trøndelag off Ørlandet, Norway on November 13, 2016. 
In a cooperative arrangement, the exterior of the Kjeungskjær Fyr or Lighthouse is protected and maintained by the Norwegian Coastal Administration. The interior has been restored and maintained by the Lighthouse Association (Kjeungen Kystlag http://www.kjeungenkystlag.no) and can be rented as adventure accommodation.

description: A bouncing ball captured with a stroboscopic flash at 25 images per second. Note that the ball becomes significantly non-spherical after each bounce, especially after the first. That, along with spin and air-resistance, causes the curve swept out to deviate slightly from the expected perfect parabola. Spin also causes the angle of first bounce to be shallower than expected.
